name: Policy Debate
aka: Policy, CX, Cross-Examination Debate, Team Policy
summary: Two teams of two argue for a year about whether the government should adopt a specific plan, using a lot of carefully researched evidence.
who: High school and college students, two to a team. In high school it is one of the National Speech & Debate Association's main events; homeschool leagues call it Team Policy. College policy debate runs through the National Debate Tournament (NDT) and the Cross Examination Debate Association (CEDA).
resolution: One policy topic for the whole school year. In high school the National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS) chooses it and the NSDA publishes it.

speeches.name: First Affirmative Constructive
speeches.speaker: 1A
speeches.job: Read the affirmative case: the problem (harms), why the present system won't fix it (inherency), the plan, and why the plan solves (solvency).

speeches.name: Cross-examination of the 1A
speeches.speaker: 1A
speeches.job: The second negative speaker questions the first affirmative speaker.

speeches.name: First Negative Constructive
speeches.speaker: 1N
speeches.job: Present the negative's off-case positions (such as disadvantages, a counterplan or topicality) and answer the case.

speeches.name: Cross-examination of the 1N
speeches.speaker: 1N
speeches.job: The first affirmative speaker questions the first negative speaker.

speeches.name: Second Affirmative Constructive
speeches.speaker: 2A
speeches.job: Answer every negative argument and extend the case.

speeches.name: Cross-examination of the 2A
speeches.speaker: 2A
speeches.job: The first negative speaker questions the second affirmative speaker.

speeches.name: Second Negative Constructive
speeches.speaker: 2N
speeches.job: Go deep on some negative positions, often while the 1NR takes the others (the "negative block").

speeches.name: Cross-examination of the 2N
speeches.speaker: 2N
speeches.job: The second affirmative speaker questions the second negative speaker.

speeches.name: First Negative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: 1N
speeches.job: Cover the positions the 2NC didn't take. Together the 2NC and 1NR are thirteen minutes of negative speaking in a row.

speeches.name: First Affirmative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: 1A
speeches.job: Answer the whole negative block in five minutes. Efficiency matters most here.

speeches.name: Second Negative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: 2N
speeches.job: Choose the negative's best path to winning, weigh it, and tell the judge why to vote negative.

speeches.name: Second Affirmative Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: 2A
speeches.job: Answer the 2NR, weigh, and tell the judge why to vote affirmative. No new arguments.

prep.note: Eight minutes of prep for each team, used in any amounts before its speeches (NSDA). College tournaments usually give more.

rewards: Deep research and careful use of evidence
Organization: answering every argument in order
Strategy: choosing which arguments to go for in the last speeches
start: Read the current NSDA policy topic and its topic analysis.
Learn the four classic stock issues (harms, inherency, plan, solvency) and topicality.
Flow a recorded round from start to finish before you debate one.
Write a short affirmative case with one plan and two advantages, then a two-page answer file to the arguments you expect.
Start at a novice division or a local league where judges expect slower speaking.
varies: Rebuttal length: most high school leagues use five minutes; some regions use four.
Prep time: NSDA gives eight minutes per team; other leagues and college tournaments set their own.
Homeschool leagues (NCFCA, Stoa) use the same 8-3-5 speech times but set their own prep time and topic, and expect speaking a lay judge can follow.
College policy (NDT and CEDA) uses longer speeches and usually about ten minutes of prep.
Speed: some circuits allow very fast speaking ("spreading"); local and homeschool leagues usually expect a conversational pace. Ask before the round.

p: The affirmative presents a plan that carries out the resolution. The negative can argue that the problem isn't real or big, that the plan won't solve it, that it would cause harms worse than it fixes (a **disadvantage**), that a different plan is better (a **counterplan**), or that the plan isn't really what the resolution calls for (**topicality**).

Each debater gives one constructive and one rebuttal and is cross-examined once. The negative's second constructive and first rebuttal come back to back, so the affirmative has to answer a lot in the 1AR.

list: **Status quo**: the way things are now, without the plan.
**Stock issues**: harms, inherency, plan, solvency (some lists add topicality).
**Disadvantage (DA)**: a bad result of the plan, with a link, an internal link and an impact.
**Counterplan (CP)**: a negative alternative that solves without the drawbacks.
**Card**: a quoted piece of evidence with its citation.
**Extend**: carry an argument forward into a later speech.
